metadata.description: Comprehensive JavaScript Interview Questions - Deep theoretical explanations with How & Why for 3.5+ years experience
metadata.usage: Import and merge with javascriptQuestionData.js or use via javascriptQuestionsMerged.js

questions.question: Explain the Event Loop in JavaScript: How does it work and why does JavaScript need it?
questions.answer: The Event Loop is the mechanism that allows JavaScript to perform non-blocking I/O despite being single-threaded. It's the backbone of async behavior in both browsers and Node.js. HOW it works: 1. Call Stack: JavaScript has one main thread with a single call stack. Synchronous code executes immediately and blocks until complete. When a function runs, it's pushed onto the stack; when it returns, it's popped off. 2. Web APIs / Libuv (Node): Async operations (setTimeout, fetch, fs.readFile, DOM events) are handed off to browser or Node APIs—they run outside the main thread. The call stack stays free. 3. Task Queues: When async operations complete, their callbacks are placed in queues: • Macrotask Queue (Task Queue): setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, UI rendering • Microtask Queue: Promise.then/.catch/.finally, queueMicrotask(), MutationObserver 4. Loop Mechanism: The event loop continuously: (a) Run one macrotask from the queue, (b) Drain ALL microtasks before taking the next macrotask, (c) Optionally render (browser), (d) Repeat. This is why Promise.then runs before setTimeout(fn, 0). WHY it exists: • JavaScript was designed single-threaded—one call stack, one thread. Without the event loop, any I/O (network, file read) would freeze the entire application. • The event loop enables non-blocking I/O: the UI stays responsive while waiting for an API response. • Microtasks have higher priority so Promise chains resolve predictably before the next timer tick—critical for framework internals (React, Vue). Edge cases: Long-running synchronous code blocks the loop—no macrotasks or microtasks run until it completes. Avoid CPU-heavy work on the main thread; use Web Workers. Performance: Microtasks can enqueue more microtasks—they're all drained before the next macrotask. A runaway microtask loop can starve macrotasks (e.g., timers never fire). Use queueMicrotask sparingly.

questions.question: Explain Closures in depth: How do they capture scope and why are they essential for encapsulation?
questions.answer: A closure is a function that retains access to its lexical scope even when executed outside that scope. The inner function "closes over" the outer environment. HOW it works: 1. Lexical Scoping: When a function is defined, it captures a reference to its surrounding scope (the environment where it was created). This is stored in the function's [[Environment]] internal slot. The scope is determined at definition time, not call time. 2. Scope Chain: When the function executes, it looks up variables in: own scope → outer function scope → ... → global. The outer scope remains in memory as long as the inner function can reference it—even after the outer function has returned. 3. Garbage Collection: Normally, when a function returns, its local variables become unreachable and are GC'd. With closures, the inner function holds a reference to the outer scope's variables, so they stay alive. This can cause memory leaks if closures hold large objects unnecessarily. WHY it matters: • Data Privacy: Create private variables—only the returned function can access them. JavaScript has no native private fields (until ES2022 #fields); closures were the original encapsulation pattern. • Partial Application & Currying: Closure captures arguments for later use. • Event Handlers & Callbacks: Handlers need access to variables from when they were created. Closures preserve that context—e.g., a click handler referencing loop variable i (common bug: use let in for-loop or pass i as parameter). • Memoization: Cache object lives in closure scope. Edge cases: Loop + closure: for (var i=0; i<3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); } prints 3 three times—i is shared. Fix: use let (block scope) or IIFE to capture i. Performance: Closures have a small memory overhead (storing scope references). Avoid closing over large objects if not needed.

questions.question: How is 'this' determined in JavaScript? Explain the four binding rules and arrow function behavior.
questions.answer: The 'this' keyword refers to the execution context—the object that invoked the function. Its value is determined at call time, not definition time. This is a common source of bugs. HOW it is determined (four rules, in priority order): 1. New Binding: When a function is called with new, this is bound to the newly created object. Highest priority. 2. Explicit Binding: call, apply, or bind—you explicitly pass this. fn.call(obj) or fn.bind(obj) sets this to obj. 3. Implicit Binding: Method invocation—obj.method(). this = the object before the dot (the "receiver"). 4. Default Binding: Standalone function call—this = global (window in browser, globalThis in Node) in non-strict mode, or undefined in strict mode. Lowest priority. 5. Arrow Functions: Do NOT have their own this. They inherit this from the enclosing lexical scope at definition time. The four rules do not apply to arrow functions. WHY it varies: • JavaScript functions are first-class—the same function can be called in different contexts. this provides a way to reference the "current" owner. • Lost this: When you pass a method as a callback (e.g., setTimeout(obj.method)), the receiver is lost—the function runs as a standalone call. Solution: bind, arrow function, or wrapper: () => obj.method(). Edge cases: Callback passed to setTimeout: this is global/undefined. Destructured method: const { log } = console; log('hi') loses this. Use arrow or bind. Real-world: React class components: bind event handlers in constructor or use arrow functions as class fields to preserve this.

questions.question: Explain the Prototype Chain and how inheritance works in JavaScript. How does it differ from classical inheritance?
questions.answer: JavaScript uses prototypal inheritance—objects inherit from other objects via the [[Prototype]] link. There is no "class" in the traditional sense; ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes. HOW it works: 1. [[Prototype]]: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] (exposed via __proto__ or Object.getPrototypeOf). When you access obj.property, the engine: (a) looks on obj, (b) if not found, looks on obj's prototype, (c) repeats until null. This is the prototype chain. 2. Constructor's prototype: Functions have a .prototype property. When you call new Foo(), the new object's [[Prototype]] is set to Foo.prototype. So Foo.prototype is the shared template for all instances. 3. Chain: obj → Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) → ... → Object.prototype → null. If a property isn't found anywhere, you get undefined. 4. Own vs Inherited: obj.hasOwnProperty('x') returns true only if 'x' exists on obj itself, not on the chain. WHY this design: • Brendan Eich modeled JS after Self (prototype-based). Simpler, more flexible—no need for class definitions upfront. • Methods on the prototype are shared; only instance-specific data lives on the object. Memory efficient—thousands of instances share one prototype. • Dynamic: You can add methods to Foo.prototype at runtime, and all existing instances get them. Comparison with classical inheritance: In Java/C++, inheritance is class-to-class. In JS, it's object-to-object. Classes in JS compile to constructor + prototype; extends sets up the prototype chain. Edge cases: Modifying Object.prototype affects all objects—avoid. Use Object.create(null) for dictionary objects with no inherited properties.

questions.question: Explain call, apply, and bind. How do they work, when to use each, and what's the performance difference?
questions.answer: These are methods on Function.prototype that let you control the 'this' value and how arguments are passed. They enable method borrowing and fixing lost context. HOW they work: 1. call(thisArg, arg1, arg2, ...): Invokes the function immediately with this = thisArg and arguments passed individually. fn.call(obj, 1, 2). 2. apply(thisArg, [args]): Same as call but arguments as a single array. fn.apply(obj, [1, 2]). Useful when you have an array of args (e.g., spreading from arguments). 3. bind(thisArg, arg1, ...): Returns a new function with this and optional args pre-filled. Does NOT invoke. const bound = fn.bind(obj); bound(); The returned function's this is permanently bound. WHY use each: • call: Invoke immediately with explicit this. Common for borrowing: Array.prototype.slice.call(arrayLike) to convert array-like to array. • apply: When args are in an array—Math.max.apply(null, arr) (or Math.max(...arr) with spread). Forwarding arguments. • bind: When you need a function to call later with fixed this—event handlers, setTimeout. Prevents "lost this." Also partial application (currying). Performance: call is slightly faster than apply (no array allocation). bind creates a new function—avoid in hot loops; use call/apply inline if possible. Modern engines optimize all three well. Alternative: Arrow functions capture this lexically—no need for bind in many cases. Spread operator replaces apply for most use cases.

questions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)? How does it work and why was it introduced?
questions.answer: The Temporal Dead Zone is the period between entering a block scope and the declaration line where let/const variables cannot be accessed—access throws ReferenceError. HOW it works: 1. Hoisting: let and const are hoisted—the engine knows they exist from the start of their block. But they are not initialized. 2. TDZ: From the start of the block until the line let x = ... runs, x is in the TDZ. console.log(x) in that window throws "Cannot access 'x' before initialization." 3. Contrast with var: var is hoisted AND initialized with undefined. You can access it (as undefined) before the line—no TDZ. let/const stay "uninitialized" until the declaration runs. 4. typeof: typeof x in TDZ also throws (unlike undeclared vars, where typeof returns 'undefined'—a security improvement to catch refs to let/const before init). WHY it exists: • Prevent use-before-declaration bugs: With var, you could accidentally use a variable before assignment, getting undefined. TDZ forces you to declare before use. • Const correctness: const must be initialized at declaration. TDZ ensures you never read it before that. • Block scoping clarity: Makes the declaration point explicit—no silent undefined from hoisting. Edge case: function foo(x = y) { let y = 2; }—y is in TDZ when default param is evaluated. Causes ReferenceError.

questions.question: Explain Promises: How do they work under the hood, and why do we need them over callbacks?
questions.answer: A Promise is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It has three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected. Once settled, the state is immutable. HOW they work: 1. Creation: new Promise((resolve, reject) => {...}). The executor runs synchronously immediately. You call resolve(value) or reject(reason) when the async work completes. 2. State: Pending → fulfilled (with value) or rejected (with reason). No other transitions. 3. Microtask Queue: .then/.catch/.finally callbacks are queued as microtasks. They run after the current synchronous code and before the next macrotask. This is why Promise.then runs before setTimeout(0). 4. Chaining: .then returns a new Promise. If the callback returns a value, the new Promise resolves with it. If it returns a Promise, that Promise's outcome is "adopted." Errors propagate down the chain until caught. 5. Error propagation: Rejected Promises propagate until .catch(). Unhandled rejections trigger unhandledrejection (and deprecation warning in Node). WHY we need them: • Callback hell: Nested callbacks become unreadable. Promises allow flat .then chains or async/await. • Composition: Promise.all (wait all), Promise.race (first wins), Promise.allSettled (all outcomes), Promise.any (first fulfilled). • Error handling: Single .catch at the end vs try-catch in every callback. Consistent. • Guaranteed async: .then always runs asynchronously (microtask), so ordering is predictable. Edge cases: Promise executor runs sync—avoid heavy work. Resolve/reject only affect first call—subsequent calls are ignored.
questions.codeExample:
const p = new Promise((res) => setTimeout(() => res(1), 100));
p.then(v => v + 1).then(console.log); // 2

questions.question: Is JavaScript pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Explain with mutation vs reassignment.
questions.answer: Technically, JavaScript is always pass-by-value—but for objects, the "value" passed is a reference (memory address). Practically: primitives by value, objects by reference. HOW it works: 1. Primitives (number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint): The actual value is copied. Changes inside the function don't affect the original. Modifying the parameter creates a new local binding. 2. Objects (arrays, functions, plain objects): The reference (pointer) is copied. Both caller and callee point to the same object. Mutating properties (obj.x = 5) affects the original. Reassigning the parameter (param = {}) does NOT affect the original—you're only changing what the local variable points to. 3. Immutability: To avoid mutating, create a copy (spread, Object.assign, structuredClone) and pass or return that. WHY this design: • Primitives are small; copying is cheap. Objects can be large; copying would be expensive. Passing a reference is O(1). • The "reference is a value" nuance: The callee cannot make the caller's variable point to a new object. The reference itself is passed by value. This prevents some bugs. Real-world: React and Redux encourage immutability—return new objects instead of mutating, so reference equality checks (===) can detect changes. Edge case: Reassigning a parameter that was an object doesn't change the original—only mutation does.

questions.question: Explain Event Bubbling and Event Capturing. How does the DOM event flow work?
questions.answer: DOM events flow through three phases: capturing → target → bubbling. Understanding this is essential for event delegation and stopPropagation. HOW it works: 1. Capturing Phase: Event travels from window down to the target element. addEventListener third argument true enables capturing. Rarely used. 2. Target Phase: Event reaches the target element. Handlers on the target run (whether registered for capture or bubble). 3. Bubbling Phase: Event travels back up from target to window. Default for most events (click, etc.). Handlers run in reverse order of capturing. 4. stopPropagation(): Stops propagation to parent/child. Doesn't prevent default (e.g., link navigation)—use preventDefault() for that. 5. stopImmediatePropagation(): Stops other listeners on the same element from firing. WHY it exists: • Event Delegation: Attach one listener on a parent; handle events from many children. Uses bubbling—child events bubble to parent. Check event.target to identify the actual element. Efficient for dynamic lists. • Historical: Netscape used capturing; IE used bubbling. W3C combined both. Bubbling is more intuitive for most use cases. Real-world: Click on a table row—delegate to , use event.target.closest('tr') to find the row. One listener for hundreds of rows. Events that don't bubble: focus, blur, load, unload, scroll (in some browsers). Use capturing if you need to catch them on ancestors.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and ===? Why does == produce unexpected results?
questions.answer: === is strict equality—compares value and type, no conversion. == is loose equality—JavaScript coerces types before comparing, leading to surprising results. HOW == coercion works (Abstract Equality): 1. Same type → SameValueComparison (like ===). 2. null == undefined → true (only pair that's equal). 3. Number vs String: string converted via ToNumber. '5' == 5 → true. 4. Boolean vs any: boolean → number (true→1, false→0). true == 1 → true. 5. Object vs primitive: object → ToPrimitive (valueOf, toString). [2] == 2 can be true. 6. Symbols never coerce—Symbol() == Symbol() is always false. WHY == is problematic: • Unexpected pairs: 0 == false, '' == false, null == undefined. Intent unclear. • Debugging: Bugs from accidental coercion (e.g., form input '' compared to 0). • Best practice: Use === everywhere. Use == only when you explicitly want null/undefined equality: value == null (catches both). Real-world: API returns numeric string "123"; strict check id === 123 fails. Prefer explicit conversion: Number(id) === 123.
questions.codeExample:
'' == 0    // true
'0' == 0   // true
false == 0 // true
null == undefined // true

questions.question: How does JavaScript's garbage collection work? Explain reachability and common memory leak patterns.
questions.answer: JavaScript uses automatic garbage collection—unreachable objects are freed. The main algorithm is mark-and-sweep (with generational collection in V8). HOW it works: 1. Reachability: Objects are reachable if they're accessible from "roots" (global variables, currently executing function's local variables, closures). The GC traces from roots and marks reachable objects. 2. Mark-and-Sweep: Mark all reachable objects. Sweep (free) everything not marked. Modern engines use generational GC: young generation (short-lived) collected often; old generation less often. 3. No circular reference problem: Unlike reference-counting, mark-and-sweep handles cycles—if A and B reference each other but nothing else references them, both are collected. WHY it matters: • You don't manually free memory. But you can create leaks by holding references to objects that should be freed. Common memory leak patterns: • Global variables: Accidentally assigning to undeclared variable creates global—never GC'd. Use strict mode. • Closures holding large objects: Inner function references outer scope—outer stays alive. Don't close over huge objects if not needed. • DOM references: Keeping reference to removed DOM nodes prevents GC. Null out refs when nodes are removed. • Timers/listeners: setInterval or addEventListener not cleared when component unmounts—callback holds closure, prevents GC. Always clear in cleanup. • Detached DOM: DOM node removed from tree but still referenced—entire subtree stays in memory. Tools: Chrome DevTools Memory profiler, Heap snapshots to find detached nodes and retained objects.

questions.question: What are WeakMap and WeakSet? When would you use them instead of Map and Set?
questions.answer: WeakMap and WeakSet hold weak references to keys—if nothing else references the key, it can be garbage collected and the entry is automatically removed. HOW they work: • WeakMap: Keys must be objects. No iteration (no keys(), values(), forEach). No size property. When the object-key is no longer referenced elsewhere, the entry is eligible for GC. • WeakSet: Values must be objects. Same weak semantics. WHY use them: • Avoid memory leaks: Storing metadata about DOM nodes—if the node is removed, Map would keep it alive. WeakMap allows GC when the node is gone. • Private data: Store instance-specific data keyed by object without preventing the object from being collected. Pre-ES2022 private fields pattern. • Caching: Cache computations keyed by object—when the object is done, cache entry can be collected. Limitations: Keys/values must be objects. No iteration, no size. You can't enumerate what's stored—by design. Real-world: React Fiber uses WeakMap to store fiber nodes keyed by DOM nodes. Vue 3 uses WeakMap for component instance metadata.

questions.question: Explain the Execution Context: What does it contain and how does it relate to scope and hoisting?
questions.answer: Execution context is the environment in which JavaScript code runs. Each function call creates a new execution context. HOW it works: 1. Components: Variable Environment (var, function declarations), Lexical Environment (let, const, block scope), this binding, outer reference (scope chain). 2. Creation Phase: Before code runs—(a) Create Variable Object / Lexical Environment, (b) Hoist var and function declarations, (c) Bind this, (d) Set up scope chain (outer reference). 3. Execution Phase: Code runs line by line. let/const are initialized at their declaration line (TDZ before that). 4. Types: Global context, function context, eval context. Each has its own Variable/Lexical Environment. WHY it matters: • Explains hoisting: var and function declarations are "moved" to the top during creation—actually, they're registered in the Variable Environment before execution. • Explains scope chain: Outer reference forms the chain for variable lookup. • Explains closures: Inner function's outer reference points to outer function's environment—stays alive. Performance: Deep scope chains (many nested functions) can slow lookup. Keep nesting shallow where possible.

questions.question: What is the difference between setTimeout(fn, 0) and queueMicrotask(fn)?
questions.answer: Both defer execution, but they use different queues and run at different times. setTimeout(fn, 0): Schedules fn in the macrotask queue. Runs after current sync code, after ALL microtasks, and after the next render (browser). Minimum delay is often 4ms (browser clamp). queueMicrotask(fn): Schedules fn in the microtask queue. Runs after current sync code, before the next macrotask. No minimum delay. Order: Sync → microtasks (all) → macrotask → microtasks → ... So queueMicrotask runs sooner than setTimeout(0). WHEN to use: • queueMicrotask: When you need "as soon as possible" after current sync code, without yielding to the browser. Similar to Promise.then timing. • setTimeout(0): When you need to yield—allow the browser to render, or defer to the next event loop tick. Useful to prevent blocking the UI. Edge case: A loop of queueMicrotask can starve macrotasks—timers and I/O never run. Use sparingly.

questions.question: When should you use Map over Object for key-value storage?
questions.answer: Object: Keys are strings (or Symbols). Has prototype chain. No guaranteed key order (modern engines preserve insertion order for string keys). No .size. JSON-serializable. Map: Keys can be any value (object, function, number). Guaranteed insertion order. .size, .has, .get, .set, .delete. Iterable. No prototype pollution. USE Map when: • Keys are objects (e.g., DOM nodes, metadata keyed by instance). • Need insertion order (e.g., LRU cache). • Frequent add/delete—Map is optimized for that. • Need .size without counting. • Want to avoid prototype pollution (user input as keys). USE Object when: • Simple string-keyed data, JSON-serializable. • Need object literal syntax, optional chaining on known keys. • Interop with APIs expecting plain objects. Performance: Map is faster for large datasets with frequent add/delete. Object is fine for small, static key sets.

questions.question: Explain the Proxy and Reflect APIs. When would you use them?
questions.answer: Proxy creates a wrapper around an object that can intercept and customize fundamental operations (get, set, has, delete, etc.). Reflect provides methods that mirror those operations and are designed to work with Proxy. HOW Proxy works: • new Proxy(target, handler). handler has "traps": get, set, has, deleteProperty, apply (for functions), construct (for new), etc. • When you access proxy.prop, the get trap runs. You can return a custom value or forward to the target. • Reflect.get(target, prop) performs the default get. Use it in traps to forward: return Reflect.get(target, prop). WHY Reflect: • Proxy handlers need to "forward" to the target for default behavior. Reflect methods do that. return Reflect.set(target, prop, value) instead of target[prop] = value (Reflect returns boolean for success). • Some operations (e.g., new) can't be done without Reflect.construct. USE cases: • Reactivity: Vue 3 uses Proxy for reactive state—intercept get/set to track dependencies and trigger updates. • Validation: Reject invalid values in set trap. • Logging: Log all property access. • Lazy loading: Return placeholder on get, load real value on first access. Performance: Proxy has overhead. Don't use for hot paths. Prefer simple objects when possible.

questions.question: How does async/await differ from Promise.then? When to use each?
questions.answer: Both handle Promises. async/await is syntactic sugar that makes async code look synchronous. .then is explicit chaining. HOW async/await works: • async function always returns a Promise. await pauses the function until the Promise settles, then resumes with the value. Under the hood, it compiles to a state machine (similar to generators). Advantages of async/await: • Readability: Sequential logic is easier to follow. • try/catch: Use try/catch for errors instead of .catch chains. • Debugging: Stack traces are clearer; you can set breakpoints on await lines. When to use .then: • Parallel execution: Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()])—you can .then to process. With await you'd do: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([...]). • When you need to return a raw Promise (e.g., from a function that doesn't need to be async). • In non-async contexts (e.g., top-level in older environments—though top-level await exists in ES2022). Best of both: async function f() { const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]); return process(a, b); } Edge case: Forgetting await—async function returns Promise, not the value. Common bug.

questions.question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy? How to implement each correctly?
questions.answer: Shallow copy: Top-level properties copied; nested objects/arrays are shared by reference. Both original and copy point to the same nested objects. Deep copy: Recursively copy all levels. Nested objects are new. Changes in the copy don't affect the original. Implementations: • Shallow: {...obj}, [...arr], Object.assign({}, obj). • Deep: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))—works for JSON-serializable data only. Fails for Date (becomes string), undefined (omitted), functions (omitted), Symbol, circular refs (throws). • Deep: structuredClone(obj)—native, handles Date, RegExp, Map, Set, typed arrays. Still fails for functions and Symbol. Handles circular refs. • Deep: lodash cloneDeep—handles more edge cases. When to use: Shallow when you won't mutate nested. Deep when you need full independence (e.g., Redux reducers returning new state). Performance: Shallow is O(n) for top-level. Deep is O(n) for full tree—slower for large objects.
questions.codeExample:
const shallow = { ...obj };
const deep = structuredClone(obj);

questions.question: Implement debounce and throttle. When would you use each?
questions.answer: Debounce: Delays execution until after a specified wait time has elapsed since the last call. Resets the timer on each call. Use for search input, window resize, form validation—execute only when user stops typing/resizing. Throttle: Ensures the function is called at most once in a specified time interval. Use for scroll handlers, mousemove, API polling—execute at regular intervals. HOW debounce works: On each call, clear previous timeout, set new timeout. When timeout fires, execute. Only the last call in a burst runs. HOW throttle works: Track last execution time. If time since last >= limit, execute and update last. Otherwise, schedule for later (or ignore). Real-world: Search: debounce 300ms—avoid API call on every keystroke. Infinite scroll: throttle scroll handler 100ms—avoid layout thrashing. Edge cases: Leading vs trailing—debounce can run on first call (leading) or last (trailing). Throttle can have leading, trailing, or both. lodash debounce/throttle support these options.

questions.question: Explain the Observer and Pub/Sub patterns in JavaScript. How do they differ?
questions.answer: Both are behavioral patterns for decoupling components. Observer: subjects notify observers directly. Pub/Sub: publishers and subscribers communicate via an event channel (broker)—they don't know each other. Observer: Subject maintains a list of observers, notifies them when state changes. Tight coupling—subject knows its observers. Example: addEventListener (DOM as subject, handler as observer). Pub/Sub: Publisher emits events to a channel; subscribers listen to channels. Loose coupling—publisher doesn't know subscribers. Example: EventEmitter, Redux (store as broker). Implementation: class EventEmitter { on(event, fn), emit(event, ...args), off(event, fn). Store { event: [fn1, fn2] }. When to use: Observer for direct 1-to-many (e.g., UI component and its listeners). Pub/Sub for many-to-many, cross-module communication (e.g., global event bus). Real-world: Vue 2 $emit (child-parent), Redux (global state), WebSocket message handlers.

questions.question: How does the V8 engine optimize JavaScript? Explain JIT compilation and hidden classes.
questions.answer: V8 uses JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation and several optimization techniques to run JavaScript efficiently. JIT: Source → parse → AST → Ignition (interpreter) generates bytecode. Hot functions are optimized by TurboFan (optimizing compiler) to native machine code. If assumptions break (e.g., type change), code is deoptimized. Hidden Classes (Shapes): V8 assigns a "hidden class" to each object based on its structure. Adding properties in the same order across instances shares the same hidden class—faster property access. Changing property order or adding dynamically creates new hidden classes—slower. Inline Caches: For property access (e.g., obj.x), V8 caches the location based on the object's hidden class. If the next object has the same shape, access is fast. Polymorphic (many shapes) = slower. Takeaways: • Initialize object properties in the same order. Avoid adding properties dynamically after creation. • Avoid changing property types (e.g., x from number to string)—triggers deoptimization. • Use monomorphic functions (same argument types) when possible.

questions.question: How would you design a system to handle 10,000 concurrent requests in Node.js?
questions.answer: Node.js is single-threaded with an event loop. To handle high concurrency: 1. Non-blocking I/O: Use async APIs (fs.promises, fetch, DB drivers with callbacks/Promises). Never use sync versions (fs.readFileSync) in request handlers—they block the event loop. 2. Connection pooling: Limit DB connections (e.g., 10–20 per instance). Use pools so connections are reused, not opened per request. 3. Horizontal scaling: Run multiple Node processes (cluster module or PM2). One process per CPU core. Load balancer distributes requests. 4. Avoid CPU-intensive work on main thread: Offload to Worker Threads for heavy computation (image processing, crypto). Or use a separate service. 5. Rate limiting & backpressure: Limit incoming requests per client. Implement backpressure for streams—don't buffer unbounded. 6. Caching: Redis for sessions, frequently accessed data. Reduce DB load. 7. Optimize event loop: Avoid long-running sync code. Break up heavy work with setImmediate or queueMicrotask to yield. Bottlenecks: Single event loop, so CPU-bound work blocks. DB connection limits. Memory (each connection holds some state).

questions.question: What is optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??)? When to use each?
questions.answer: Optional chaining (?.): Short-circuits if the left side is null or undefined. obj?.a?.b returns undefined instead of throwing if obj or obj.a is null/undefined. Also works for optional calls: fn?.(). Nullish coalescing (??): Returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined. Unlike ||, 0 and '' are NOT replaced—they're valid. a ?? b → a if a is not null/undefined, else b. When to use ?.: Safe nested access when any part might be null/undefined. Replaces verbose if (obj && obj.a) checks. When to use ??: Default values when 0 or '' should be preserved. count ?? 0 gives 0 only when count is null/undefined. count || 0 would replace 0 with 0 (same here) but would replace '' with default—use ?? when that matters. Precedence: ?? has lower precedence than && and ||. Use parentheses: (a && b) ?? c.
questions.codeExample:
user?.address?.city;
const count = input ?? 0;

questions.question: What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
questions.answer: for...in: Iterates over enumerable property keys of an object (including inherited). Returns keys as strings. Use for plain objects. Can include prototype properties—use hasOwnProperty to filter. for...of: Iterates over iterable values (arrays, strings, Map, Set, arguments, NodeList). Uses [Symbol.iterator]. Use for collections. Throws if target is not iterable. Key difference: for...in gives keys; for...of gives values. Gotchas: for...in on array gives indices as strings, and can include enumerable non-index properties. Prefer for...of for arrays. for...of on plain object throws—objects are not iterable by default.
questions.codeExample:
for (const k in {a:1}) {}  // k = 'a'
for (const v of [1,2,3]) {} // v = 1, 2, 3

questions.question: Explain Object.defineProperty and property descriptors. How does Vue 2 use them for reactivity?
questions.answer: Object.defineProperty lets you define or modify a property with fine-grained control over writable, enumerable, configurable, and get/set. Descriptor types: • Data descriptor: value, writable, enumerable, configurable. • Accessor descriptor: get, set, enumerable, configurable. Configurable: If false, you can't delete the property or change its descriptor (except value if writable). Vue 2 reactivity: Vue walks the data object and uses defineProperty to add getters/setters for each property. getter collects the current watcher as a dependency; setter notifies watchers when the value changes. Limitations: can't detect new properties (Vue.set) or array index assignment—Vue overrides array methods. Vue 3: Uses Proxy instead—can intercept any property access/change, supports new properties and arrays natively.
questions.codeExample: Object.defineProperty(o, 'x', { value: 1, writable: false });

questions.question: What are tagged template literals? Give a real-world use case.
questions.answer: Tagged templates are function calls with template literals: tag`Hello ${name}!`. The tag function receives an array of string fragments and the interpolated values. Signature: function tag(strings, ...values). For `Hello ${name}!`, strings = ['Hello ', '!'], values = [name]. The function can return anything (string, object). Use cases: • Sanitization: Escape user input to prevent XSS. tag checks values and escapes HTML. • Styled-components: CSS-in-JS—tag processes template to generate unique class names and inject styles. • i18n: Translate string fragments, replace placeholders with localized values. • SQL builders: Sanitize values to prevent injection, build parameterized query. Raw strings: tag receives strings.raw for unescaped strings (e.g., \n as backslash-n).

questions.question: What is the Module pattern? How does it relate to ES modules?
questions.answer: Module pattern (IIFE): (function() { let private = 1; return { get() { return private; } }; })(). Creates closure for private state; returns public API. Pre-ES6 way to encapsulate. ES Modules: import/export. Each file is a module with its own scope. Static structure—imports are resolved at parse time. Enables tree-shaking. Async loading with dynamic import(). Differences: ES modules are native, statically analyzable, support tree-shaking. IIFE runs at runtime, can't be statically analyzed. ES modules are the standard; use them in modern projects. IIFE still used in legacy scripts or non-module environments.

questions.question: Explain the difference between static and instance methods in JavaScript classes.
questions.answer: Instance methods: Defined on the prototype. Called on instances (obj.method()). Have access to this (the instance). Static methods: Defined with static keyword. Live on the constructor. Called as Class.method(). No this to instance—used for utilities, factory methods, or methods that don't need instance data. Examples: Array.isArray (static), Array.prototype.map (instance). Object.keys (static). Static properties: static count = 0—shared across all instances. Useful for caching, config. Private static: static #secret—shared but not accessible from outside the class.

questions.question: What is the Singleton pattern in JavaScript? When is it appropriate?
questions.answer: Singleton ensures only one instance of a class exists and provides a global point of access. Implementation: Use a module (ES module or IIFE) — the module is evaluated once, so the exported object is the single instance. Or: store instance in a variable, return it on subsequent constructor calls (and make constructor private in languages that support it—JS doesn't, so convention or Symbol). In Node/ES modules: const db = new Database(); export default db; — the module is cached, so db is a singleton. When appropriate: Database connection, logger, config, cache. One shared resource. When to avoid: Singletons create hidden dependencies and make testing harder (can't easily replace with mocks). Prefer dependency injection when possible.

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined? When should you use each?
questions.answer: undefined: Variable declared but not assigned; missing property; function with no return; optional param not passed. Type: 'undefined'. null: Intentional absence of value. You assign it explicitly. Type: 'object' (historical quirk). Both are falsy. Use value == null to check for both (== null is true for null and undefined). When to use: undefined = "not set" / default. null = "explicitly empty" / no result. APIs often use null for "no result" (e.g., document.getElementById). Use undefined for optional params; null when clearing a value.
questions.codeExample:
let a; console.log(a); // undefined
let b = null; // explicitly empty

questions.question: Explain Generator functions: How do yield and next() work, and when would you use generators?
questions.answer: Generator functions are functions that can pause and resume execution, yielding multiple values over time. They return an iterator (generator object) with a next() method. HOW it works: • function* gen() { yield 1; yield 2; }. Calling gen() returns a generator object; it does NOT run the function body yet. • next() resumes execution until the next yield. Returns { value, done }. value is the yielded value; done is true when the function returns. • yield pauses and passes a value out. next(arg) can pass a value back in—it becomes the result of the yield expression. WHY use generators: • Lazy iteration: Generate values on demand (infinite sequences). • Async flow control: Before async/await, libraries like co used generators for async code. yield Promise, resume when it resolves. • Custom iterators: Simpler than implementing [Symbol.iterator] manually. Real-world: Redux Saga uses generators for side effects. Infinite sequences: function* naturals() { let n=0; while(true) yield n++; }

questions.question: How do you implement memoization? What are the trade-offs?
questions.answer: Memoization caches function results keyed by arguments to avoid redundant computation. Implementation: Higher-order function that wraps fn. Use a Map (or object) keyed by stringified arguments. On call, check cache; if hit, return. Else compute, store, return. Key considerations: • Cache key: JSON.stringify(args) for simple args. For objects, key order matters. Custom key function for complex args. • Cache size: Unbounded cache can grow—use LRU (Least Recently Used) for production. • Pure functions only: Memoization assumes same inputs → same output. No side effects. When to use: Expensive computation (fibonacci, recursive algorithms), API response caching (with TTL). Trade-offs: Memory for speed. Stale data if inputs can change (e.g., date). Not for non-deterministic or side-effectful functions.

questions.question: What are first-class functions? Why does this matter in JavaScript?
questions.answer: First-class functions mean functions are treated like any other value—they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from functions, and stored in data structures. Implications: • Callbacks: Pass functions to setTimeout, array methods (map, filter), event handlers. • Higher-order functions: Functions that take or return functions (map, reduce, debounce). • Closures: Functions can capture outer scope because they're values that persist. • Functional patterns: Currying, composition, partial application. Comparison: In C, functions are not first-class—you pass function pointers but can't easily create or return functions. JavaScript's design enables the functional and callback-heavy style that powers modern JS.

questions.question: What is the Factory pattern vs Constructor pattern? When to use each?
questions.answer: Constructor: function Person(name) { this.name = name; } + new Person('A'). Creates instance with [[Prototype]] = Person.prototype. Requires new—forgetting it can cause bugs (this = global). Factory: function createPerson(name) { return { name, greet() { ... } }; }. Returns plain object. No new, no this. Simpler, more flexible. When Constructor: When you need prototype-based inheritance, instanceof checks, shared methods on prototype. OOP style. When Factory: When you want encapsulation (private variables via closure), flexibility (return different types based on args), or avoid new. Composition over inheritance. Modern: ES6 class is syntactic sugar over constructor + prototype. Factory + Object.create for prototypal inheritance without constructors.

questions.question: Explain the difference between slice() and splice(). Why does splice mutate?
questions.answer: slice(start, end): Extracts a portion of an array. Returns NEW array. Does NOT mutate. end is exclusive. Negative indices count from end. O(n) for the slice. splice(start, deleteCount, ...items): Modifies the array in place. Removes deleteCount elements from start, optionally inserts items. Returns array of removed elements. Mutates the original. WHY splice mutates: Historical design—it was intended for in-place editing. Many array methods (push, pop, shift, unshift, sort, reverse) mutate. Prefer non-mutating alternatives (slice, spread, concat) when you need immutability (e.g., React state). Gotcha: splice and slice have similar names but opposite mutability. slice = safe copy; splice = destructive edit.

questions.question: How does try-catch handle synchronous vs asynchronous errors?
questions.answer: Synchronous: try-catch catches errors thrown in the try block. Works as expected. Asynchronous: try-catch does NOT catch errors in callbacks or Promises that reject later. The try block has already completed when the async callback runs. Example: try { setTimeout(() => { throw new Error(); }, 0); } catch(e) {} — catch never runs. For Promises: Use .catch() on the Promise chain, or await inside async function and wrap in try-catch. await throws on rejection, so try-catch works. For async/await: try { await promise; } catch (e) { } — catches rejection because await suspends and resumes in the same async context. Unhandled rejections: Promises that reject without .catch trigger unhandledrejection. In Node, this can crash the process (configurable).

questions.question: What is the Call Stack? How does it relate to stack overflow and recursion?
questions.answer: The Call Stack is a LIFO data structure that tracks function calls. When a function is called, its execution context is pushed onto the stack. When it returns, it's popped. HOW it works: f() calls g() which calls h(). Stack: [f, g, h]. When h returns, stack: [f, g]. When g returns, stack: [f]. Single-threaded JS has one call stack. Stack overflow: Recursion without a base case (or very deep recursion) keeps pushing. Stack has a limit (~10k–100k frames depending on engine). Exceeded → RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Tail call optimization (TCO): ES6 specified TCO for tail recursion—the compiler could reuse the stack frame. But only Safari implemented it; Chrome/V8 removed it. So deep recursion can still overflow. Use iteration or trampoline for very deep recursion. Async and the stack: When an async callback runs, it starts a fresh stack. The original stack is gone. That's why stack traces for async errors can be truncated.
questions.codeExample: function recurse() { recurse(); } // Stack overflow

questions.question: Explain the difference between Object.freeze, Object.seal, and Object.preventExtensions.
questions.answer: Object.preventExtensions: Prevents adding new properties. Can delete and modify existing. Object.isExtensible(obj) → false. Object.seal: preventExtensions + makes all existing properties non-configurable (can't delete, can't change descriptor). Can still modify property values if writable. Object.freeze: seal + makes all data properties non-writable. Values can't be changed. Nested objects are NOT frozen—shallow only. For deep freeze, recurse. Order of restrictiveness: preventExtensions < seal < freeze. When to use: freeze for immutable config objects. seal when you want to lock structure but allow value updates. preventExtensions rarely used alone. Performance: Engines can optimize objects that are sealed/frozen (no need to check for property addition).

questions.question: What is the difference between forEach, map, and reduce? When to use each?
questions.answer: forEach: Iterates, executes callback for each element. Returns undefined. Use for side effects (logging, DOM updates). Cannot break—use for...of if you need break. map: Transforms each element, returns NEW array. Use when you need a transformed array. Callback should be pure (no side effects) for predictability. reduce: Reduces array to single value (or object, array). accumulator, currentValue, index, array. Use for sums, flattening, grouping, any aggregation. More general than map/filter—can implement both with reduce. Performance: All are O(n). for loop can be faster for very hot paths (no function call overhead). Prefer declarative (map/filter/reduce) for readability unless profiling shows a need for for loop. Chain: arr.filter(...).map(...).reduce(...) — readable. Each creates intermediate array—for large data, consider single reduce to avoid multiple passes.

questions.question: How would you implement a simple Promise from scratch (Promises/A+ compliant)?
questions.answer: A minimal Promise must: 1. States: pending, fulfilled, rejected. Once settled, no transitions. 2. Executor: Runs synchronously. resolve(value) and reject(reason) change state and trigger callbacks. Ignore if already settled. 3. then(onFulfilled, onRejected): Returns new Promise. If pending, store callbacks. If settled, queue microtask to run callback. Handle thenable (object with then method)—adopt its state. 4. Value propagation: If onFulfilled returns value, resolve returned Promise with it. If throws, reject. If returns Promise, adopt its outcome. 5. Microtask: Use queueMicrotask (or equivalent) to run callbacks asynchronously. Key details: then must return a new Promise. Callbacks must run in separate microtask. Resolution must handle circular thenables (avoid infinite loop). Full spec: Promises/A+.
